ut.title: Ultrasonic Thickness Testing & UT Inspection | Anchorage, AK
ut.description: Ultrasonic thickness testing and UT weld inspection in Anchorage, AK for fuel tanks, piping, vessels and port steel. Technicians mobilized. Request a quote.
ut.h1: Ultrasonic Testing (UT) Inspection in Anchorage, Alaska
ut.html:
Atlantis NDT performs ultrasonic testing in Anchorage, Alaska: wall-thickness surveys on fuel and process tanks, piping and pressure vessels, and angle-beam examination of structural and pressure welds. Technicians are mobilized to your terminal, plant or yard with calibrated instruments and cold-weather couplants, and every reading is reported against the code you name. Describe the equipment through the Anchorage UT inspection quote request and we reply within one business day.

Where ultrasonic testing is used in Anchorage

Anchorage is Alaska's freight and fuel gateway, and that shapes the steel in and around it. The Don Young Port of Alaska handles most of the non-petroleum cargo shipped into the state outside Southeast, and roughly nine tenths of the liquid fuel that reaches Southcentral Alaska. The port operates petroleum terminals, a cement terminal, dock cranes, and about three million barrels of liquid fuel storage, connected by pipelines to tank farms and to truck and rail loading racks. Ted Stevens Anchorage International Airport is one of the busiest cargo hubs in the world, and the Alaska Railroad has been part of the city's economy since it was founded. Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson sits next to the port.

Every one of those systems contains metal that loses wall to corrosion. Fuel tank shells and roofs, product piping, loading rack headers, pump manifolds, heat exchangers and boiler vessels all need periodic thickness checks. Marine environments add salt, and cold climates add condensation inside insulation, where corrosion under insulation develops out of sight. Ultrasonic thickness testing reaches through the wall without cutting the insulation off the whole system, which is why it is the standard first look.

What ultrasonic testing finds and what it does not

The probe sends a pulse and times its return. For thickness, the round trip through the wall, converted with the known sound velocity of the material, gives the remaining metal. For a weld, an angled beam sweeps the joint volume and reflects off lack of fusion, cracks, slag and incomplete penetration. The method is good at what it measures directly and poor at what it infers, so the report states the readings and the limits, not guesses.

In Anchorage the limits show up in specific ways. Frost, ice and frozen condensation on a surface block the sound path, so the surface must be thawed and dry. Thick coatings and rough, rusted plate scatter the beam. Austenitic stainless piping welds and cast components need special procedures. Pitted walls are the classic trap: one reading at the bottom of a pit can look healthy while another point a few millimeters away is nearly through. The survey pattern and the lowest reported value must therefore be read together. Floor plates in tanks are another limit, since an accessible spot reading is not a floor map.

Tank farm and port thickness work in Anchorage

The most common request is thickness readings on aboveground tanks and their piping. Shell courses are measured in vertical lines at several heights, with extra points around nozzles, manways, the lowest course and any area where staining or coating failure shows moisture. Roof plates and roof supports are checked where the structure is safe to reach. Where the owner follows API 653, the owner's authorized inspector chooses the locations, evaluates the results and sets the next interval. Atlantis does not take that role. We take the readings, document the instrument and calibration and hand over a clear table of points below the required minimum.

Product piping and loading rack headers follow API 570 or ASME B31.3 principles, with condition monitoring locations measured repeatedly so the owner can calculate a corrosion rate. Depending on service, pipelines connected to a terminal may also fall under the federal pipeline safety rules in 49 CFR Parts 192 or 195, and the owner's integrity group decides which applies. Dock cranes and cargo equipment at the port are mostly a magnetic particle subject, which our Anchorage MT page explains, but their pressure components and welded pedestals can need UT.

Codes and acceptance criteria

ASME Section V, Article 4, covers ultrasonic examination of welds, Article 5 covers materials, and the contact thickness practice appears as SE-797 in Article 23. ASTM E797 is the consensus standard for contact pulse-echo thickness measurement and ASTM E164 covers weldments. ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 12 governs ultrasonic examination of welds when the construction code calls for it. AWS D1.1 applies to structural steel and carries its own ultrasonic acceptance classes, and AWS D1.5 applies to bridge steel. API 510, 570 and 653 organize in-service inspection of vessels, piping and tanks, with the owner's authorized inspector responsible for the program.

The acceptance criteria always come from the governing document or the owner's specification. When a weld is examined under one code and the owner would prefer another, the choice is agreed in writing before the job. The report states the table, the measured size and the decision.

Alaska's mechanical inspection program and what UT contributes

Alaska's Labor Standards and Safety Division runs a Mechanical Inspection section that oversees boilers and unfired pressure vessels in commercial and public structures. Commissioned state inspectors or authorized insurance inspectors carry out the inspections, and a state certificate of operation is required, with some exemptions. The codes the division lists include the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code, the API pressure vessel inspection code and the National Board Inspection Code. Elevators and other devices have their own track, with the Municipality of Anchorage handling inspections and permits in its own jurisdiction.

None of that changes what a UT survey is for. The state or insurance inspector decides compliance, and Atlantis provides measured thickness, weld examination results and the code reference behind each decision. Where a vessel repair is made, the National Board Inspection Code expects documentation, and the examination record is part of it. Industrial sites under OSHA's process safety management rule, 29 CFR 1910.119(j), also schedule mechanical integrity inspections around recognized good practice.

How the technique is applied in cold conditions

For thickness on corroded steel the technician uses a dual-element probe, calibrated on a step block of the same material, and checks the calibration again at the end. The waveform stays on the screen so a doubled echo or a lamination cannot pass as a thickness. In Alaska winters, equipment has its own demands: batteries lose capacity in the cold and are kept warm in an inner pocket, display screens slow down, and cables stiffen. Couplant must be one rated for low temperatures, because a standard gel stiffens or freezes on a cold wall. Calibration blocks are kept near the temperature of the part, since the code limits how far apart they may be, and the technician records both temperatures.

Weld work uses angle beams of 45, 60 or 70 degrees on a reference block with side-drilled holes to set a distance-amplitude curve. Scanning from both sides where access allows, the technician sizes any reflector and records its position relative to the weld centerline. In a heated enclosure around a pipe joint, the temperature of the steel may still differ from the air, so surface readings with a contact thermometer are routine.

Who performs and reviews the work

Technicians are qualified under the Atlantis written practice, which follows ASNT SNT-TC-1A. The person holding the probe is a Level II who calibrates, scans and interprets, and an ASNT Level III approves procedures and reviews reports. Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT, signs off on procedure approvals. Atlantis is certified to ISO 9001 and ISO 14001. Customer contracts that name another qualification scheme should say so in the inquiry. For procedure writing, see Level III consulting and written practice development.

What the Anchorage UT report contains

The report identifies each component by tag or drawing, the procedure and revision, the instrument, probe and block, the couplant, the surface condition and the surface temperature. For thickness work it lists readings in a grid by location, alongside the nominal and required minimum thickness when the owner supplies them, and flags every point below the minimum. For weld work it records the beam angle, reference level, scan coverage, each indication's position, length and amplitude, and the accept or reject decision against the stated criteria. Areas that could not be scanned, such as welds under supports, are listed as limitations. The technician's name, level and the date close the report so the inspector can rely on it directly.

Planning an ultrasonic job in Anchorage

Season and daylight shape the plan. From late fall into spring, steel temperatures sit far below freezing, and outdoor work depends on wind shelters, heated tents and warm breaks for people and instruments. Short winter days limit what can be done outside, and snow and ice on tank roofs and shell walkways must be cleared before anyone climbs. Summer has long daylight and milder weather, which makes it the busy season for outdoor tank and port work, so booking early matters. Insulation must be removed or windowed for piping, and ice inside an insulation window must be cleared before readings are taken.

Access to the port and the airport zone involves security credentialing, which takes planning time and should be set up before travel. Because Atlantis has no office in Anchorage, technicians travel to your site for the agreed scope, and the flights, lodging and winter gear are part of the mobilization plan. A drawing set with numbered locations and clear access notes does more to keep the job on schedule than any other preparation.

UT compared with MT and PT for an Anchorage job

Use UT when the question is wall thickness or an internal flaw. Use magnetic particle inspection for surface cracks in carbon steel, such as crane hooks, pins and attachment welds, and read the Anchorage MT page. Use liquid penetrant testing for stainless steel and aluminum, on the Anchorage PT page. The national ultrasonic testing page, the ultrasonic testing guide and the Article 5 explanation carry the wider detail, and statewide scope sits on the Alaska inspection services page.

Training your own ultrasonic technicians

Remote and seasonal sites often prefer an in-house person for routine thickness checks. Our UT Level 1 training and UT Level 2 training are available with simulator practice, and your employer certifies the technician under its own written practice. See the Anchorage NDT training page for how delivery works.

faq.q: Can you measure fuel tank wall thickness in Anchorage in winter?
faq.a: Yes, with low-temperature couplant, warmed batteries and frost removed from the test surface. Calibration is checked on a block kept near the part temperature. Extreme cold or wind may call for a shelter or a schedule change.

faq.q: Does Atlantis replace the API 653 or 510 inspector?
faq.a: No. The owner's authorized inspector remains the inspector of record and decides remaining life and intervals. Atlantis performs the examination and reports readings, calibration records and any points below minimum thickness.

faq.q: What does the state of Alaska require for boilers and pressure vessels?
faq.a: Alaska's Mechanical Inspection section oversees boilers and unfired pressure vessels, using commissioned state inspectors or authorized insurance inspectors, and a certificate of operation is generally required. Confirm exemptions and your equipment status with that division.

faq.q: Can ultrasonic testing find corrosion under insulation?
faq.a: It measures the wall once the technician can reach the metal, usually through an inspection window in the jacketing. It does not scan through thick insulation, so locations are chosen where moisture is likely and windows are opened for readings.

faq.q: What should I send for an Anchorage UT quote?
faq.a: Send equipment tags or drawings, material and nominal thickness, coating or insulation, surface condition, the governing code, site access and security requirements, and your target dates. A numbered location list shortens the scoping.

faq.q: Does frost or ice affect ultrasonic readings?
faq.a: Yes. Ice or frozen condensation blocks the sound path and gives false readings or none. The surface must be cleared, thawed and dry, and the couplant must be rated for the surface temperature.

faq.q: Can UT be used instead of radiography on welds in Alaska?
faq.a: Only where the governing code and the owner permit it. Some codes allow ultrasonic examination of production welds and others require radiography. The method is agreed with the owner, engineer and inspector before work starts.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have an office in Anchorage?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no office in Anchorage. Crews fly in for the agreed scope, and travel and winter logistics are planned into the job. Start with the quote request.

faq.q: Can my Alaska team be trained to take UT readings?
faq.a: Yes. Level 1 and Level 2 courses are available with simulator practice. Your company certifies each person under its written practice, and we can help review or write that written practice.

mt.title: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MT) in Anchorage, AK | MPI
mt.description: Magnetic particle inspection (MT) in Anchorage, AK for port cranes, steel piles, lifting gear and welds, with cold-weather procedures. Request a quote.
mt.h1: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MT) in Anchorage, Alaska
mt.html:
Atlantis NDT provides magnetic particle inspection in Anchorage, Alaska, for dock and yard cranes, lifting gear, steel piles, structural welds and machinery. Technicians travel to your site with yokes, particles, thermometers and cold-weather procedures, examine ferromagnetic steel to a written procedure, and report indications against the criteria you specify. Send the component list through the Anchorage MT inspection quote request and we reply within one business day.

Where magnetic particle inspection is used in Anchorage

Alaska's cargo comes ashore in Anchorage. The Don Young Port of Alaska reports about five and a half million tons of fuel and cargo a year, and its general cargo terminals depend on dock cranes, roll-on and roll-off ramps, and heavy handling equipment that lifts and lowers all day. Cargo cranes carry hooks, spreader beams, shackles, sheave pins and welded boom and portal structure, and each can develop fatigue cracks that grow under load. The port is also in the middle of a modernization program with new terminal construction, which brings steel piles, pile splices and structural welds.

Away from the dock, the airport cargo apron, rail yards and industrial sites around the city use ground handling equipment, loading rack steelwork, pipe supports and storage tank attachments. Military and utility work adds more heavy steel. In a city where parts are not just a truck ride away, finding a crack before it becomes a failure is a straightforward way to avoid a long outage, and MT is the quickest surface method for carbon steel.

What MT detects and what it misses

Magnetized steel leaks flux at any crack that breaks the surface or lies very near it, and fine iron particles collect at the leakage to draw the crack in ink or in fluorescent light. The method detects fatigue cracks, weld toe cracks, laps and seams in ferromagnetic material, and it shows them to the technician's eyes in place.

It will not test austenitic stainless steel, aluminum, copper or other nonmagnetic metals, for which penetrant testing is the surface method, as the Anchorage PT page describes. It cannot see deep internal flaws and cannot measure wall loss. Two things surprise people: a crack lying parallel to the field is nearly invisible, which is why every area is magnetized in two directions, and a thick coating or heavy scale can hide a fine crack, so surfaces are cleaned or coatings are limited to the thickness the procedure allows.

Codes and acceptance criteria for MT work in Anchorage

ASME Section V, Article 7, governs the method: magnetizing equipment, particles, field verification, procedure content and interpretation. Acceptance is from the construction code. Pressure vessels built to ASME Section VIII Division 1 use Mandatory Appendix 6, process piping built to ASME B31.3 uses its acceptance table, structural steel built to AWS D1.1 uses its own criteria, and bridge steel under AWS D1.5 has its own provisions. ASTM E709 is the guide behind many procedures and ASTM E1444 is the practice many purchase specifications call out.

Waterfront structures and piles are usually specified by the owner or engineer, who should name the code edition, the extent of examination and the criteria in the scope. When the specification is silent, ask before the first weld is cleaned, because an arbitrary standard produces a report nobody can use.

Alaska oversight, lifting equipment and the MT record

Alaska's Mechanical Inspection section oversees boilers and unfired pressure vessels through commissioned state inspectors or authorized insurance inspectors, and repairs follow the National Board Inspection Code. A documented MT examination of a repaired weld is a normal part of that record. Cranes and lifting devices fall under the owner's maintenance program and federal workplace safety expectations, and owners usually schedule hook and pin examination into annual or seasonal shutdowns. The owner decides interval and disposition. Atlantis performs the examination and flags anything that needs engineering review or code inspection.

How the technique is applied

Most field work uses an electromagnetic yoke. An AC yoke must lift at least 10 pounds at the pole spacing used and a DC or permanent-magnet yoke at least 40 pounds, and the technician proves this with a test weight at the start of the job. Dry powder works on rough or warm surfaces, visible wet particles in a can give more sensitivity, and fluorescent particles under ultraviolet light give the most. Prods suit large welds and castings but need care to avoid arc burns. After examination, parts are demagnetized only when leftover magnetism would harm welding, machining or bearings, and the remaining field is checked with a meter.

Cold changes the practical details. Wet particle carriers thicken, aerosol cans lose pressure, gloves hide fine indications, and yoke legs can ice up. For wet methods, the particle suspension must be kept above the temperature limits stated in the procedure, and jobs are often done inside a heated shelter. The procedure should state the lowest steel temperature at which it has been demonstrated, and a calibrated contact thermometer is used to confirm it, because a wind chill reading is not a surface temperature.

Cold-weather limits and how a procedure handles them

This is where Anchorage differs from most US cities, so the method deserves a plain explanation. A standard written procedure is demonstrated within a stated temperature range. Below that range, one of three things must happen: the part is warmed, the work moves into an enclosure, or the procedure is demonstrated at the lower temperature on a known-flaw reference block and approved by a Level III. Local heating with a torch is not a fix on its own, because uneven heating, moisture from combustion and surface contamination can ruin sensitivity. Heated enclosures with calibrated thermometers are safer and easier to document.

The report records the surface temperature at the time of examination and the procedure used, so a reviewer can see that the temperature limits were met. Fluorescent work inside an enclosure also solves the lighting problem, because the black light needs a darkened area, and Alaska daylight, whether endless in July or scarce in December, rarely cooperates.

Typical findings on port and yard steel

Some defects turn up again and again around a waterfront. Fatigue cracks start at the toes of welds that join padeyes, lugs and brackets to girders, and in the fillet radii of pins and shafts. Hooks crack at the throat. Corrosion pits at the base of a weld can act as starting points for cracks, so a cleaned weld that shows pitting deserves a closer look than its length alone suggests. Impact damage from cargo handling leaves gouges and cold-worked metal, and repair welds that cooled too fast develop cracks in the heat-affected zone. Piles driven into hard ground can show weld splice cracks where the hammer energy concentrated. Knowing these habits lets the technician decide where to set the yoke legs, instead of sweeping across the whole structure at random.

Corrosion protection adds a practical wrinkle. Marine coatings on cranes and piles are often thick, and the procedure limits how much coating the field can tolerate before sensitivity falls. The simplest answer is to remove the coating at the weld toes and examine bare metal, then have the owner recoat. Where the owner prefers to keep coating on, the technician can demonstrate the procedure at the actual coating thickness on a known-flaw block before the real examination begins.

Who performs and reviews the MT work

Technicians are qualified under the Atlantis written practice, which follows ASNT SNT-TC-1A. A Level II sets up the equipment, performs the examination and interprets indications, and an ASNT Level III approves the procedure and reviews reports, including any cold-weather demonstration. Anoop Rayavarapu is ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. Atlantis is certified to ISO 9001 and ISO 14001. Where a customer names another qualification scheme, it should be stated in the request. For procedures and written practice help, see Level III consulting.

What the Anchorage MT report contains

The report names the component or weld by tag or drawing number, the procedure and revision, and the surface condition. It lists the magnetizing method and equipment, the yoke lift check or current used, particle type and color, the white-light or black-light readings where relevant, the surface temperature and the directions of magnetization. Every indication is described by location, orientation and length, compared with the stated acceptance criteria and given a plain accept or reject result. Sketches or photographs identify the exact spot. The report finishes with the technician's name, level and date, and lists any area that could not be examined, such as a weld hard against a wall.

Planning a magnetic particle job in Anchorage

Plan around weather and access. In winter, short days, wind and sub-freezing steel make heated shelters worth their cost, and snow and ice must be removed from cranes, platforms and walkways before anyone climbs. In summer, long daylight and mild weather make outdoor work easier, and the port and contractors are busy, so schedule early. Crane work needs lockout, tagout and a clear lift plan, and the owner usually sets the order of the work so cargo operations are not interrupted.

Port and airport areas require security credentials that take time to arrange, so request them before travel. Because the company keeps no office in the city, a crew is mobilized from outside Alaska, and flights, lodging and cold-weather gear are part of the plan. Surfaces need cleaning, and any coating should be identified in the inquiry so the thickness can be checked against the procedure limits.

MT compared with PT and UT for an Anchorage job

Pick MT for surface cracks in carbon steel, such as crane parts, piles and attachments. Pick penetrant for stainless and aluminum on the Anchorage PT page. Pick ultrasonic testing for wall loss and internal flaws on the Anchorage UT page. A pile or crane job often uses both: UT on the groove welds and MT on the fillets. The national magnetic particle testing page, the complete MT guide and the Article 7 explanation have more detail, and the statewide view sits on the Alaska inspection services page.

Training your own MT technicians

Operators with their own cranes and shops often train an in-house technician. Our MT Level 1 training and MT Level 2 training teach yoke practice and indication interpretation, and the MT training overview describes the format. Your employer certifies the technician under its written practice, and the Anchorage NDT training page explains delivery.

faq.q: Can you perform magnetic particle inspection on port cranes in Anchorage?
faq.a: Yes. Technicians travel to the site and examine hooks, pins, boom and portal welds and other ferromagnetic components, then report indications against the owner's criteria. The owner decides interval, repair and return to service.

faq.q: Does cold weather stop MT in Alaska?
faq.a: It limits it, but does not stop it. Parts can be warmed, work can move into a heated enclosure, or the procedure can be demonstrated at the lower temperature on a reference block and approved by a Level III.

faq.q: Can MT inspect steel piles and pile splices?
faq.a: Yes, where the piles are accessible and ferromagnetic. The owner or engineer specifies the code and extent, often AWS D1.1 for the welds. Coatings must be checked against the procedure limits.

faq.q: What magnetizing equipment do you bring?
faq.a: A calibrated electromagnetic yoke with a test weight to prove its lifting power, dry powder, visible and fluorescent wet particles, a black light, white-light meter, contact thermometer and field indicators, with prods when the specification calls for them.

faq.q: Do you demagnetize parts after MT?
faq.a: When leftover magnetism would interfere with later welding, machining or bearing service, or when the specification asks. The technician demagnetizes and checks the residual field with a meter.

faq.q: Which code sets MT acceptance on my welds?
faq.a: The construction code or owner specification does, such as ASME Section VIII Appendix 6, ASME B31.3, AWS D1.1 or AWS D1.5. The report quotes the criterion used for each decision.

faq.q: Does MT work on stainless steel and aluminum?
faq.a: No. MT only works on ferromagnetic materials such as carbon and low-alloy steel. Stainless steel and aluminum are examined with liquid penetrant testing instead, which Atlantis also performs on site.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have an office in Anchorage?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no office in Anchorage. Technicians travel to your site for the agreed scope and travel is planned into the job. Use the quote request to describe what needs examining.

faq.q: Can my crew learn MT for our own crane program?
faq.a: Yes. Level 1 and Level 2 courses are available, and your company certifies each person under its own written practice following SNT-TC-1A. Atlantis can also help write or review that written practice.

pt.title: Liquid Penetrant Testing (PT) in Anchorage, AK | Dye PT
pt.description: Liquid penetrant testing in Anchorage, AK for stainless, aluminum and steel welds and fittings, with cold-weather procedures. Mobilized technicians. Request a quote.
pt.h1: Liquid Penetrant Testing (PT) in Anchorage, Alaska
pt.html:
Atlantis NDT provides liquid penetrant testing, also called dye penetrant inspection, in Anchorage, Alaska. It is the surface method for stainless steel, aluminum, nickel alloys and any non-porous material that magnetic particles cannot test. Technicians travel to your site, clean the surface, test it under a written procedure that addresses cold conditions, and report indications against the criteria you set. Send the parts or welds through the Anchorage PT inspection quote request and we reply within one business day.

Where penetrant testing is used in Anchorage

Anchorage is a port, an air cargo hub and a rail terminus, and each runs equipment built from nonmagnetic metals. Stainless steel appears in process piping, heat exchangers, food and water handling, and fuel system fittings. Aluminum appears in aircraft ground support equipment, vessels, marine fixtures, trailers and structural frames. Salt air, de-icing chemicals and cold cycling punish welds on all of them, and cracks that start at a weld toe or a fitting radius are invisible until they leak. Penetrant testing is the practical way to find them.

Typical Anchorage work includes stainless piping welds and nozzle connections after repair, aluminum fabrications and fittings, valve bodies and pump parts from the port's fuel systems, small pressure vessels, and welded repairs on mixed-material equipment. Because PT does not depend on magnetism, one procedure can handle a stainless weld, an aluminum casting repair and a carbon steel nozzle in the same visit, as long as each surface is prepared for its own material.

How penetrant testing works and what it cannot see

A thin, low-viscosity liquid is applied to a clean surface and allowed to seep into any opening for a stated dwell time. The surface liquid is then removed, a fine white developer is applied, and the developer pulls the trapped liquid back to the surface as a bright line or dot. Color-contrast penetrants are read in white light, and fluorescent penetrants are read under ultraviolet light in a darkened area, with higher sensitivity.

Only discontinuities open to the surface can be found. A crack closed by smeared metal, paint, corrosion product or machining debris takes no penetrant, so cleaning decides the result. Porous surfaces hold penetrant everywhere and produce a background that hides real indications. Internal flaws and wall loss require ultrasonic testing, covered on the Anchorage UT page. Penetrant also has to be removed from parts that enter oxygen, food or hydraulic service, so the final cleaning step matters as much as the first.

Codes and acceptance criteria

ASME Section V, Article 6, defines penetrant methods: material forms, cleaning, dwell, removal, developer application and interpretation. Acceptance comes from the construction code. ASME Section VIII Division 1 vessels use Mandatory Appendix 8, and ASME B31.3 piping uses its acceptance table. ASTM E165 is the general industry practice that many specifications reference, and AWS D1.1 uses visual criteria with penetrant as a supplement where the specification requires it. Stainless and nickel alloy specifications commonly limit halogens and sulfur in the penetrant materials, so certified lots are used and recorded in the report.

The owner or engineer sets the criteria, and the technician evaluates against them. If a specification is silent, ask before testing begins. A report that quotes the wrong acceptance table is worse than no report, because someone will rely on it.

Alaska oversight and the records PT supports

Alaska's Mechanical Inspection section oversees boilers and unfired pressure vessels, and inspections are performed by commissioned state inspectors or authorized insurance inspectors. Repairs to stainless and alloy pressure equipment follow the National Board Inspection Code, and a penetrant examination of the repaired weld is a common requirement. The inspector of record, state or insurance, decides acceptance of the repair. The PT report is the evidence that inspector reviews. Under OSHA's process safety management rule, 29 CFR 1910.119(j), industrial sites also document mechanical integrity inspections, and a surface-crack examination of a repaired fitting belongs in that record.

Cold-weather penetrant testing: the part everyone asks about

Penetrant materials are designed for moderate temperatures. The ASME procedure assumes the part and the materials sit within a defined band, with its lower edge just above freezing, and sub-freezing steel is far outside it. At low temperature penetrant becomes thick, flows slowly into cracks, and may freeze in them. Developer can clump. Water-based cleaners freeze outright. The same cold that makes people hurry makes penetrant less reliable, so rushing is the wrong response.

There are three honest routes. The first is to bring the part inside a heated enclosure and let it come up to temperature, which is the safest and the easiest to document. The second is to warm the area gently and verify the surface temperature with a contact thermometer before and during the examination. The third is a procedure demonstrated at the lower temperature on a comparator block with a known set of cracks, approved by a Level III. Local torch heating is not recommended, because it causes uneven surfaces and combustion moisture. The report records the surface temperature and the procedure used, so a reviewer can verify that the limits were respected.

How the technique is applied

The sequence begins with cleaning. Oil and grease are removed with solvent, scale and paint are removed mechanically, and the surface is dried fully. Penetrant is applied by spray or brush and left for the dwell the procedure requires. Solvent-removable visible-dye systems are the usual field choice, because they need no power or water, and the excess is wiped with a clean cloth and then lightly dampened with solvent. After drying, a thin, even coat of developer is applied. The technician watches the surface as the developer works and again at the end, because the growth of a bleed-out tells the severity of a flaw. Indications are measured, photographed and recorded, and the surface is cleaned of residue after testing.

Stainless and aluminum surfaces need extra care. Carbon steel wire brushes embed iron in stainless and can start corrosion, so brushes are dedicated by material. Aluminum is soft and smears under wire brushing, hiding cracks. When mechanical cleaning has been used on aluminum, a light etch may be needed to reopen the surface before testing.

Materials and residues that matter in Alaska

Several details separate a sound penetrant job from a poor one. Penetrant, remover and developer should come from one family and one manufacturer, because mixing products can cause chemical reactions that wash out indications. Stainless steel and nickel alloy work needs low-halogen and low-sulfur materials, with the batch numbers recorded. Aerosol cans lose pressure in the cold, so they are kept warm in a coat pocket or a heated truck until used. Rags must be lint-free, and solvent must be kept off hot surfaces. Disposal of used penetrant and rags follows the site's waste rules.

Corrosion also leaves its own marks. Salt deposits on marine equipment dry into crusts that block flaws, and they must be washed off with fresh water and the part dried before any penetrant goes on. Aluminum oxide, weld spatter and old paint have the same effect. A cleaned weld that still shows dull patches in the light usually has more surface preparation ahead of it. None of this is exotic, but it is the difference between seeing a crack and writing a report that says none was found because the surface was not ready.

Who performs and reviews the PT work

PT examinations are performed by technicians qualified under the Atlantis written practice, following ASNT SNT-TC-1A. A Level II performs the work and evaluates indications, and an ASNT Level III approves the procedure, including any low-temperature demonstration, and reviews reports. Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT, signs off. Atlantis is certified to ISO 9001 and ISO 14001. If a contract names a specific qualification scheme, state it in the request. See Level III consulting for procedure development.

What the Anchorage PT report records

The report names the component, the material and the surface tested, with the procedure and revision. It lists the penetrant system, manufacturer and lot numbers of penetrant, remover and developer, the cleaning method, the surface and ambient temperatures, the dwell and developing times, and the lighting level used for reading. Indications are described by location, type and size, with a plain accept or reject statement against the stated criteria. Sketches or photographs accompany any rejectable indication. The technician's name, level and date close the report, and any area not testable is listed as a limitation.

Planning a penetrant job in Anchorage

Treat temperature as the main schedule driver. In winter, plan an enclosure, a heater and a thermometer, and leave time for parts to warm through, since a steel pipe can hold cold long after the air around it feels comfortable. In summer the problem is milder, though shaded work is still easier than direct sun on a dark surface. Daylight matters for color-contrast work, and dark winter afternoons make lighting an issue in unheated yards. Wind blows dust onto wet developer and spoils it.

Port and airport areas require security credentials that take time to arrange. The company has no office in the city, so a crew is mobilized with its own gear, and the plan includes flights, lodging and winter clothing. Tell us the material, coating and weld type when you request a quote, and if the parts can be brought to a heated shop, the job gets simpler.

PT compared with MT and UT for an Anchorage job

Choose PT for stainless steel, aluminum and other nonmagnetic metals, or where geometry makes magnetizing awkward. Choose MT for carbon steel such as crane parts and piles; see the Anchorage MT page. Choose UT for wall thickness and internal flaws. Training your own penetrant technicians

Penetrant testing is often the first method a maintenance team learns. Our PT Level 1 training and PT Level 2 training cover theory and practice, with the PT simulator for repetition, and the PT training overview describes the format. Your employer certifies the technician under its written practice, and the Anchorage NDT training page explains how delivery works.

faq.q: Can penetrant testing be done in Anchorage winters?
faq.a: Yes, with controls. Parts are warmed or tested inside a heated enclosure, surface temperature is confirmed with a thermometer, or a procedure is demonstrated at the lower temperature and approved by a Level III.

faq.q: Why does cold weather matter for liquid penetrant testing?
faq.a: Penetrant thickens and flows slowly into cracks when cold, and cleaners and developer may freeze or clump. The code assumes a moderate band of temperature, so colder work needs a qualified procedure or warming.

faq.q: Is PT suitable for aluminum and stainless steel?
faq.a: Yes. Both are nonmagnetic, so penetrant is the usual surface method. Stainless and nickel alloy work often limits halogens and sulfur in the penetrant materials, and lot numbers are recorded.

faq.q: What cleaning is needed before penetrant testing?
faq.a: Oil, grease, scale and paint must be removed and the surface dried completely. Wire brushing aluminum can smear metal over cracks, so a light etch or different cleaning may be needed first.

faq.q: Who decides if an indication is acceptable?
faq.a: The construction code or owner specification sets the criteria, such as ASME Section VIII Appendix 8 or ASME B31.3. The technician evaluates against them and the report states which criterion was used.

faq.q: Can you test fittings from a fuel system?
faq.a: Yes, for surface-breaking cracks in nonporous fittings, valve bodies and welds. Parts must be cleaned of residue afterward, especially those returning to oxygen, hydraulic or food service.

faq.q: Can PT replace MT on carbon steel?
faq.a: It can find surface cracks in carbon steel, but MT is usually faster and more sensitive there. Penetrant is chosen when the part is nonmagnetic, when magnetizing is awkward, or when the specification calls for it.
